lead: Every multimedia file is built from a small set of digital units. A character is a code number, a drawing is a list of commands, an image is a grid of pixels, a sound is a sequence of samples, and a video is a sequence of frames. Once you know the unit and its size, you can estimate storage and transmission needs before writing any code. This chapter defines those units and separates media that have a time axis from media that do not.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 digital images and sampling, and Chapter 4.1 for multimedia elements.

blocks.text: Media are grouped by whether they change with time. Text, graphics and images are non-temporal (discrete) media: a page, logo or photograph can be shown and held. Audio, video and animation are temporal (continuous) media: their meaning depends on playback over time. Some syllabi call these 'discrete' and 'continuous' media. Every medium has a digital unit. Text uses a character code. Vector graphics use a drawing command such as 'line to (x, y)'. An image uses a pixel value. Audio uses a sample. Video uses a frame. The unit fixes how size is counted: characters, commands, pixels, samples or frames. A presentation can mix both families: a narrated slide has non-temporal text and temporal audio, kept aligned by synchronization (see Chapter 4.9). Knowing the unit lets you estimate storage before compression; compression only reduces the count (see Chapter 4.6).

Text is stored as character codes, not as pictures. ASCII maps 128 characters to 7-bit codes; extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 256 codes. Unicode assigns a code point to characters in most writing systems; UTF-8 stores a code point in 1 to 4 bytes. For plain English, ASCII is enough. For Hindi, Tamil or mixed scripts, Unicode is required. A font is the visual design of glyphs. A bitmapped font stores each glyph as a small pixel pattern for one size; scaling it makes edges jagged. An outline font stores lines and curves plus hints; the rasterizer fills pixels at the requested size, so it stays sharp. Use bitmap fonts for tiny fixed displays, outline fonts for documents and screens. Text size depends on characters and encoding: a page of 2,000 ASCII characters is about 2 kB before formatting. The font file is separate from the text file.

sections.h3: Graphics and images: commands and pixels

blocks.text: Graphics and images both produce pictures but store different units. Vector graphics store drawing commands: move to a point, draw a line or curve, fill a shape, set colour and width. The renderer turns commands into pixels at the display resolution. A raster image stores a grid of pixels. Resolution is the grid size, such as 640×480 pixels. Colour depth is bits per pixel; with d bits, each pixel can take one of 2^d values. A 24-bit RGB pixel uses 3 bytes, one byte each for red, green and blue. Raw image size is W×H×d÷8 bytes, before headers. A 1,000×1,000 image at 24 bits is 3,000,000 B, or 3 MB with 1 MB = 10^6 B. Vector art stays sharp when enlarged because commands are re-rendered; a raster image shows pixel blocks when enlarged beyond its grid. Vector suits logos, charts and fonts; raster suits photographs and scanned pages. File formats are separate (see Chapter 4.4); colour models are in Unit 1.

sections.h3: Audio and video: samples and frames

blocks.text: Audio is a continuous pressure wave. An analog-to-digital converter samples the wave at a sampling rate f_s, measured in hertz (sample times per second per channel), and rounds each sample to a bit depth b. With b bits there are 2^b quantization levels. Channels N_ch is 1 for mono and 2 for stereo. The Nyquist rule: to reconstruct a signal up to frequency f_max, sample above twice f_max, so f_s > 2 f_max. Human hearing reaches about 20 kHz; 44.1 kHz satisfies this with room for filters. A higher bit depth reduces quantization noise but increases raw size. Compressed audio and perceptual coding come later (see Chapter 4.7). Video is a sequence of frames. Frame rate is frames per second (fps); resolution is frame width×height; colour depth is bits per pixel. Progressive video draws every line of each frame. Interlaced video splits a frame into two fields, odd lines then even lines; it saves bandwidth on old television but shows combing on fast motion. Raw sizes use the formulas below.

blocks.where: R_audio is raw audio bytes per second; f_s is samples per second per channel; N_ch is number of channels; b is bits per sample; 8 bits = 1 byte.

blocks.text: S_frame = W × H × (d ÷ 8),   R_video = S_frame × F
blocks.where: S_frame is bytes per frame; W and H are width and height in pixels; d is bits per pixel; F is frames per second; R_video is raw video bytes per second.

examples.question: A one-minute stereo recording uses 44.1 kHz and 16 bits per sample. A video frame is 640×480 pixels at 24 bits per pixel and plays at 25 frames/s. Find the raw audio size in MB, the raw size of one frame in MB, and the raw video data rate in MB/s. Use 1 kB = 1000 B and 1 MB = 10^6 B.
steps: Audio: b = 16 bits = 2 bytes per sample. f_s = 44,100 samples/s per channel, N_ch = 2.
Frame: d = 24 bits = 3 bytes/pixel. One frame bytes = 640 × 480 × 3 = 921,600 B = 0.9216 MB.
Video rate = 921,600 B/frame × 25 frames/s = 23,040,000 B/s = 23.04 MB/s.
examples.answer: One minute of stereo audio is 10.584 MB; one frame is 0.9216 MB; the raw video rate is 23.04 MB/s.

sample_rate = 44100

traps: Sampling rate is per channel. Stereo at 44.1 kHz stores two samples at each sample time, so total samples per second is 88,200, not 44,100.
Do not mix bits and bytes. A 16-bit sample is 2 bytes; a 24-bit pixel is 3 bytes.
Video rate needs frames per second. A frame size in MB is not a data rate; multiply by fps.
Nyquist says greater than twice the highest frequency, not equal to it. 44.1 kHz is chosen above 40 kHz for 20 kHz audio.
Non-temporal does not mean 'not digital'. Text, graphics and images can be files; they simply have no playback time axis.

quiz.q: What is the difference between non-temporal and temporal media? Give one example of each.
quiz.a: Non-temporal media have no playback time axis; examples are text, graphics and images. Temporal media are played over time; examples are audio, video and animation.

quiz.q: Why does an outline font stay sharp when enlarged while a bitmapped font becomes jagged?
quiz.a: An outline font stores lines and curves; the rasterizer computes pixels at the requested size. A bitmapped font stores fixed pixels for one size, so scaling stretches those pixels and shows jagged edges.

quiz.q: A mono recording uses 22.05 kHz and 8-bit samples. Find the raw bytes for 30 seconds. Use 1 kB = 1000 B.
A 320×240 RGB frame at 24 bits per pixel is shown at 15 fps. Find the raw frame size in kB and the data rate in MB/s. Use 1 kB = 1000 B and 1 MB = 10^6 B.
A signal has components up to 12 kHz. Is 20 kHz sampling enough? Justify using Nyquist.
quiz.a: No. Nyquist requires f_s > 2 × 12 kHz = 24 kHz. The 20 kHz rate is below 24 kHz, so aliasing can occur.

quiz.q: Why is image colour depth measured in bits per pixel, while audio bit depth is measured in bits per sample?
quiz.a: An image stores one colour value for each pixel, so its precision is bits per pixel. Audio stores one quantized amplitude value for each sample, so its precision is bits per sample.

quiz.q: A 10-second stereo clip uses 48 kHz and 24 bits. Find its raw size in MB. Compare it with a mono 16-bit clip at the same rate and duration. Use 1 MB = 10^6 B.
quiz.a: Stereo 24-bit byte rate = 48,000 × 2 × 3 = 288,000 B/s. Size = 2,880,000 B = 2.88 MB. Mono 16-bit byte rate = 48,000 × 1 × 2 = 96,000 B/s. Size = 960,000 B = 0.96 MB. The stereo 24-bit clip is three times the size.

beyond: Not for the exam. In web systems, the word media type also appears in HTTP Content-Type and CSS media queries, where it means a data format or device class, not a multimedia time axis. Industry pipelines encode each medium with a codec, package streams in a container, and adapt bitrate to the network. Search for MIME types, codec, container, and adaptive bitrate streaming to connect this chapter to practice.
